title: Security Since Wi-Fi 6
summary: WPA3 closes WPA2’s weak points, Wi-Fi 6E requires it in 6 GHz, and Wi-Fi 7 builds on it.

opener.promise: Stronger sign-in for shared-password and staff networks alike
opener.problem: A guessable WPA2 password can be cracked offline; devices can be fooled by fake access points.

beats.heading: WPA2: two doors, two weak points

caption.headline: [[wpa2|WPA2]]: two doors, two weak points
caption.takeaway: A guessable shared password can be cracked offline; a [[fake-access-point|fake access point]] can fool devices.

beats.body:
Hospitals run two kinds of Wi-Fi sign-in through the same [[access-point|access points]]. Many clinical device networks use one shared password: [[wpa-personal|WPA2-Personal]]. Staff devices usually sign in with their own credentials: [[wpa-enterprise|WPA2-Enterprise]].

Each has a weak point. Someone in the parking lot can record a device joining the shared-password network and try millions of guesses offline {{wpa3-sae}}. On the staff network, a device that is not set up to check the sign-in server can be fooled by a [[fake-access-point|fake access point]] {{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}.
beats.bottomLine: Both kinds of WPA2 network can be attacked quietly: one through a recorded sign-in, the other through a convincing fake.
beats.sceneDescription: A hallway wall on a hospital unit with two doors under an access point: a keypad door for the shared-password network, with an infusion pump in front, and a badge door for staff sign-in, with a workstation. An outsider copies a recorded sign-in from the keypad and carries it to a desk, where the lock pops open. At the staff door, the workstation is linked to a red fake access point instead of the real one.

callout.title: WPA2’s two weak points
points: Shared password: a recorded sign-in lets attackers guess offline{{wpa3-sae}}
Staff sign-in: certificate checks depend on device configuration{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}

beats.heading: WPA3 closes both weak points

caption.headline: [[wpa3|WPA3]] closes both weak points
caption.takeaway: Recordings can’t be guessed offline{{wpa3-sae}}, and staff devices must check the network is genuine{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}.

beats.body:
[[wpa3|WPA3]]-Personal replaces the shared-password handshake with [[sae|SAE]]: a recording is useless for offline guessing, so every guess must be tried live against the real network {{wpa3-sae}}. Each session also gets a fresh key, so a password leaked later cannot unlock traffic recorded earlier {{wpa3-forward-secrecy}}.

WPA3-Enterprise makes devices check the sign-in server’s certificate before trusting it {{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}, so a fake access point cannot pose as the hospital. WPA3 became required for new Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices {{wpa3-mandatory-cert}}.
beats.bottomLine: WPA3 closes the most common ways attackers break hospital Wi-Fi sign-in, and current devices already support it.
beats.sceneDescription: Back at the keypad door. The outsider’s recording turns into a sealed gray box that gives nothing to test, and their single live guess at the real keypad is refused. The infusion pump gets its own key for the session.

callout.title: What WPA3 changes
points: Shared password: a recording gives nothing to guess offline{{wpa3-sae}}
Staff sign-in: devices must check the server is genuine{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}
Each session gets a fresh key{{wpa3-forward-secrecy}}

questions.q: We already use WPA2-Enterprise. What do we gain from WPA3?
questions.a: Mandatory certificate checks{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}, and in Only mode protected control messages{{wpa3-ent-pmf-required}}. Your sign-in server and credentials usually carry over; devices and access points need WPA3 support.

questions.q: What about guest Wi-Fi with no password?
questions.a: Wi-Fi Enhanced Open encrypts each guest device’s traffic without a password{{owe-what}}, so an open network is no longer readable by anyone nearby.

beats.heading: 6 GHz and Wi-Fi 7 make WPA3 the baseline

caption.headline: Wi-Fi 6E and 7: WPA3 required
caption.takeaway: In 6 GHz and on Wi-Fi 7, WPA3 is required{{wpa3-6ghz-required}}{{wpa3-mlo-required}}; older devices use a separate network.

beats.body:
**Wi-Fi 6E** brought the first band with no WPA2 at all: secured networks in 6 GHz use WPA3, and open guest networks use Enhanced Open {{6ghz-security-options}}. Staff networks there run WPA3-Enterprise Only mode {{wpa3-ent-6ghz-eht}}, which requires protected control messages {{wpa3-ent-pmf-required}}.

**Wi-Fi 7** goes further: multi-link connections require WPA3 {{wpa3-mlo-required}}, and Wi-Fi Alliance guidance adds stronger encryption and protects the announcements an access point broadcasts {{wifi7-eht-security}}. Devices that cannot do WPA3 can stay on a separate, older network while they are replaced {{wpa3-dual-ssid-legacy}}.
beats.bottomLine: Moving to 6 GHz and Wi-Fi 7 makes the strongest settings the baseline. WPA3 is one layer of security, not a complete program.
beats.sceneDescription: Above both doors, the access point is labeled Wi-Fi 7 and 6 GHz, WPA3 sign-in. An older phone that supports only WPA2 is turned away from the main doors and moves to a smaller side door, a separate network for older devices, labeled as one migration option. A note shows what the earlier generation accepted.

callout.title: What changes on 6E and 7
points: 6 GHz: WPA3 or Enhanced Open, never WPA2{{6ghz-security-options}}
Older devices: a separate network is one option{{wpa3-dual-ssid-legacy}}

questions.q: Will our older clinical devices still connect?
questions.a: Devices without WPA3 cannot join 6 GHz networks{{wpa3-6ghz-required}} or Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connections{{wpa3-mlo-required}}. Many will stay on 2.4 and 5 GHz on a separate network name{{wpa3-dual-ssid-legacy}} until they are replaced.

questions.q: Does WPA3 make our network compliant?
questions.a: No single feature does. WPA3 is one layer of security; it complements network segmentation, device management and your organization’s security and compliance processes.

cisco.text: A Cisco network offers Wi-Fi 7 only when its security meets the requirements; otherwise access points run it as Wi-Fi 6 or 6E{{cisco-noncompliant-downgrade}}. Beacon protection turns on automatically for compliant networks{{cisco-beacon-protection-auto}}, and Cisco’s Wireless Configuration Analyzer Express includes a readiness check{{cisco-wifi7-readiness-check}}.

keyFigures.note: Earlier generations have no multi-link operation.

lineage.lead: A separate Wi-Fi Alliance security program, not part of one generation.

sinceWifi6.wifi6: WPA3 becomes required for new Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices{{wpa3-mandatory-cert}}.
sinceWifi6.wifi6e: In 6 GHz, no WPA2: WPA3, or Enhanced Open for guests{{6ghz-security-options}}.
sinceWifi6.wifi7: Multi-link connections require WPA3{{wpa3-mlo-required}}, with stronger encryption and protected beacons{{wifi7-eht-security}}.
